newsitem.title: USA: US bank economists see 2.0 percent growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: US bank economists see 2.0 percent growth in 1997.

text.p: A group of bank economists on Wednesday predicted that the U.S. economy would grow at an annual rate of 2.0 percent in 1997.

But, the Economic Advisory Committee of the American Bankers Association cautioned, "any small variation from this trend ... would create significant challenges for policy makers at the Federal Reserve."

The group said that given the tightness of U.S. labor markets, even growth that is slightly above 2.0 percent could create enough wage and inflation pressures to force the Fed to raise interest rates.

On the other hand, the group said that with the economic expansion about to enter its seventh year, business and consumer pent-up demand may be largely satisfied, which could mean slightly slower growth and may even provide flexibility for the Fed to lower rates.
While the group saw growth averaging 2.0 percent over the course of 1997, it pegged fourth quarter over fourth quarter growth at 2.1 percent.
Turning to consumer prices, it saw an increase of 3.0 percent on average. It projected an average unemployment rate of 5.5 percent.
Turning to the dollar, the consensus forecast was for a dollar/yen rate of 115 on average for the last month of 1997 and a dollar/mark rate of 1.57.

The group gave its economic forecast after meeting Tuesday with the members of the Federal Reserve Board. However, Joel Naroff, chairman of the ABA economists' panel, stressed that the group's expectations for Fed policy were based strictly on the members' forecasts and not what was said in the meeting.
Asked what the group projected for the outcome of the upcoming Feb 4-5 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, Naroff said the expectation was no change in interest rates.

Naroff overall described Fed policy as being on a "knife's edge," given the challenges of determining the appropriate policy at a time when minor variations in growth could present such different outcomes for inflation and interest rates.
